name: Carlos Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a campaign coordinator at a sportswear brand, mostly running shoes and gym kit. My day is the email calendar: I write the promo emails, build the segments, check the discount codes work, and line up the in-store posters with the website. Around four I sit with the regional sales people and they tell me what didn't sell.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst part of that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is launch mornings, when a new shoe drops and you watch the orders come in live. The worst is writing basically the same email forty times with tiny changes for each country. I use a subject-line tool now and then, mostly because my manager Ines said everyone should try it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds quite comfortable, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit, but politely. At work I'd joke that the robots aren't coming for the running shoe emails after all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if AI stalls, my biggest problem goes back to being a sales target for running shoes, which honestly I can live with. The forty versions of the same email might get a bit quicker, and that's fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and push for the senior coordinator role that opens next spring. I'd keep putting four hundred a month into my index fund. Maybe I'd learn the subject-line tool properly, since it would still be around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, actually. Daniel and I could stop having this conversation over dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop having this conversation. What does it usually sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel teaches history at a secondary school, and he says his job's safe because teenagers need a human to roll their eyes at. Then he asks if mine is, and I change the subject.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sales targets. Sportswear is up and down, and if a season flops, juniors are the first ones asked to do more for the same pay. That's not AI, that's just retail.

say: I'd joke that the robots **aren't coming** for the running shoe emails.
I'd say I **told you so**, but politely, to friends who were worried.
think: I think my main problem goes back to **sales targets**, which I can live with.
I'd expect the forty near-identical **country emails** to get a little quicker.
do: Push for the **senior coordinator** role that opens next spring.
Keep putting **four hundred** a month into my index fund and learn the subject-line tool properly.
feel: **Calm** and pleased, with one less worry at the dinner table.
S0.quote: If AI stalls, my biggest problem goes back to being a sales target for running shoes, which honestly I can live with.
fieldNote: His **money** and many local jobs make this picture genuinely secure for him.
The only pressure he names is **seasonal sales**, which he sees as normal retail.
He's **open to tools** once they're proven, unlike more resistant colleagues.

steps.text: Apply for the senior coordinator role opening next spring
Keep paying four hundred a month into his index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more or less what my manager is already hinting at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies should share the gains with workers, not just cut the junior roles. I'd probably post about it on a professional site and get three likes from people I went to university with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the bit of my job I do best is the bit that goes. I use the subject-line tool maybe twice a week, and I already know it writes better subject lines than I do. The emails, the segments, the code checks, all of that is exactly the thinking work on the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a proper course in the AI email tools at work, so I'm the one running them, not the one replaced by them. I'd join the creative workers' union, because I want someone at the table when they decide who goes. And I'd hold back on the new flat Daniel and I were looking at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's not panic, it's more like a stone in my shoe all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Felix, who does the country versions with me. He's even more junior than me, and his whole job is the translation-and-tweak work. If they cut one of us, it's probably him first, then me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold back on the flat. How much were you planning to spend?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd saved about thirty thousand between us for a deposit. I'd keep it in the account for another year instead, just in case one of us needs it.

say: I'd say firms should **share the gains** with workers, not just cut juniors.
I'd post it on a **professional site** and expect few likes.
think: I think the part I do best, **email copy**, is what goes first.
I believe the subject-line tool already **writes better** than I do.
do: Take a proper **course** in the AI email tools at work.
Join the **union** and keep our flat **deposit** in savings another year.
feel: **Anxious**, like a stone in my shoe all day, but not panicked.
S1.quote: I use the subject-line tool maybe twice a week, and I already know it writes better subject lines than I do.
fieldNote: He's honest that the tool **beats him** at his own core task.
He worries for **Felix**, the colleague below him, before himself.
He pairs **learning the tools** with joining a union, mixing adaptation and protection.

steps.text: Take the company course on AI email tools
Keep the thirty thousand flat deposit saved another year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wow. Okay. Two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need a basic income and a tax on the companies selling this stuff. I'd go to marches, and I'd mean it this time, not just share a post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd lose my job, probably within a year of it arriving. My work is all screens and thinking, and the robots three years later don't matter for me. My partner teaches teenagers in a classroom, so for once I'd be the one asking him how to keep a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the index fund payments and keep cash, because I'd want to see the money. I'd look at a one-year teacher training course right away, since classrooms feel more human. And I'd talk to my parents about whether we could all lean on each other if it got bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the floor tilted. I'd sleep badly, I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your parents. What would leaning on each other actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They run a small print shop, and print is already dying. So maybe it's me helping them with savings, not the other way round. That's a strange thought at 27.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would teacher training even be safe, with AGI that fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Probably not completely. But there's something about a room of fourteen-year-olds that I think people will still want a human in front of.

say: I'd call for a **basic income** and a tax on the firms selling AI.
I'd go to **marches** this time, not just share posts.
think: I think I'd **lose my job** within a year, because it's all screens.
I'd see robots arriving three years later as **no help** for me.
do: Stop **index fund** payments and keep my savings as cash.
Apply for a **one-year teacher** training course straight away.
feel: **Alarmed**, like the floor tilted, and sleeping badly.
S2.quote: My partner teaches teenagers in a classroom, so for once I'd be the one asking him how to keep a job.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** within a year and says it plainly.
His parents' **print shop** is already shrinking, so family support may flow from him.
He bets on **classrooms** staying human, while admitting he isn't sure.

steps.text: Pause index fund payments and hold savings as cash
Apply for a one-year teacher training course
March for a basic income and an AI tax
Talk with his parents about sharing money if things get bad

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's still fast, but it's a different kind of fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a window and we're wasting it if governments don't start retraining people now. At work I'd push the union to get a deal on notice periods.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I could try teaching, but I'd be walking into a school while the same machines walk in behind me. Still, it's enough time to test it before I jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get really good at the AI email tools for the first couple of years, because that's what keeps me paid. Then I'd do the teacher training around 2028 and start in a school before 2031. I'd keep the flat deposit in savings until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. I'd still check the news too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably business studies or media. Daniel thinks I'd be good at it because I'm patient with the regional sales team, which is a low bar but I'll take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the school plan didn't work, what's the fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't have one yet. Maybe something with the union, organising. I'd have a few years to find out.

say: I'd say we have a **window** and governments waste it without **retraining** now.
I'd push the union for proper **notice periods**.
think: I think **teaching** could work, though the same machines may follow me in.
I'd use five years to **test** the switch before jumping.
do: Master the **AI email tools** for two years to stay paid.
Do **teacher training** around 2028 and keep the flat **deposit** saved.
feel: **Anxious** but with a plan, and checking the news too often.
S3.quote: Five years means I could try teaching, but I'd be walking into a school while the same machines walk in behind me.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **sequence** things: tools first, retraining second.
He has **no fallback** if teaching fails, and admits it.
His **progressive** outlook shows in pushing the union for notice deals.

steps.text: Become the team's expert on the AI email tools
Keep the flat deposit in savings until 2031
Push the union for longer notice periods

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds almost manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time to do this fairly, so there's no excuse. I'd say it at work too, carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is long enough to be careful, and being careful is the thing I'm actually good at. I'd still expect the email job to go before 2036, but I'd have time to move on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the senior coordinator role first and learn the AI tools as they come in. I'd buy the flat with Daniel in the next year or two, since his teaching pay is steadier. Around 2030 I'd start teacher training, and I'd keep the index fund going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, maybe still a bit anxious. It's a long way off, but it's coming for my bit of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said buying the flat. Isn't that a risk if your job goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but Daniel's job is safer than mine and the mortgage would be on both of us. I'd want it fixed for ten years so I know the number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a 20-year-old choosing marketing now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a 20-year-old to pick something where people need you in the room, and do marketing on the side if they love it.

say: I'd say a decade leaves **no excuse** for doing this unfairly.
I'd raise it **carefully** at work, without sounding alarmist.
think: I think ten years suits me, because being **careful** is my strength.
I'd still expect the **email job** to go before 2036.
do: Go for **senior coordinator** and learn the AI tools as they arrive.
Buy the **flat** with my partner and start **teacher training** around 2030.
feel: Mostly **uneasy**, with some anxiety because my work is still in the path.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to be careful, and being careful is the thing I'm actually good at.
fieldNote: He still expects to **lose the email job**, so the mood stays anxious.
He leans on his partner's **steadier income** to justify buying the flat.
His advice to the young is to choose work where **people need you** in the room.

steps.text: Apply for the senior coordinator role
Learn each new AI email tool as it arrives
Buy a flat with a ten-year fixed mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be one of the first out and there'd be no time to retrain properly. What would help is paid retraining that starts before you lose the job, not after, and companies being made to give a year's notice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the boring work. Nobody at a sportswear brand gets into marketing to write the same email forty times, but that email is how juniors like me learn. If that goes, I'm not sure how anyone becomes senior.

headlineQuote: Nobody at a sportswear brand gets into marketing to write the same email forty times, but that email is how juniors like me learn.
portrait: Carlos is a 27-year-old **campaign coordinator** at a sportswear brand who writes promo emails.
He lives with Daniel, a history teacher, and has **strong savings** plus an index fund.
He uses AI tools **now and then** and admits they already beat him at subject lines.
He moves from calm to **alarmed** at two years, then plans a careful shift into **teaching**.
He backs a union and **basic income**, and worries about juniors like his colleague Felix.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be among the first out with no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** that starts before job loss, and a **year's notice** from employers.
